performers: Soojin Han, violin; Hankyung Arte Philharmonic; Seokwon Hong, conductor
question: How does a slow movement grow out of a held note?
intro: The Andante follows the first movement without a break: a bassoon holds the B of the last chord, then steps up to C. Follow a lyrical C major theme, a darker A minor middle section in which the violin plays melody and tremulous accompaniment at once, and a serene return. The file ends where the score runs on into the finale. All three movements of this set come from one live concert.

Middle section · A minor, orchestra then violin
Return · the lyrical theme in C major
sections.mNote: main lyrical theme returns in C major

cues.title: A held B joins the movements
cues.text: There is no break after the first movement. The bassoon sustains its B from that movement’s last chord before moving up a semitone to middle C, which turns E minor into the lyrical C major of the Andante. This file begins on the held B; a short wind introduction follows before the soloist enters.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia describes the bassoon’s B moving up to C and the absence of a break between movements; the score (printed pp. 27–28) runs the movements together, with the held bassoon B, then a flute line and other winds over low strings, the soloist resting until the theme starts. The bass pitch class is B at 0:00–0:15, G at 0:25, B at 0:30 and C at 0:35; the level is −21.4 dB at 0:00 and −34.2 dB at 0:05. The chroma cannot separate the bassoon.

cues.title: C major settles
cues.text: By 0:35 the bass has reached C and the music is in C major, the key of the lyrical theme. From about 0:40 the sound brightens and detected note activity rises from nothing to three or four a second, as the soloist’s theme begins over a moving accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is C major (0.85–0.94) from 0:35 to 1:20; the centroid rises from 1,373 Hz at 0:35 to 2,140 Hz at 0:40 and the detected onsets from 0.0 to 3.4–3.8 per second at 0:40–0:45; the report has boundaries at 0:12 (0.97) and 0:24 (0.87). The score (printed p. 28) starts the solo theme after the introduction.

cues.title: A theme in long breaths
cues.text: Between about 0:45 and 1:20 the level stays within a few decibels near −24 dB while the accompaniment keeps moving. Listen for the melody holding long notes above that motion: Wikipedia likens the movement to one of Mendelssohn’s own Songs Without Words.
cues.evidence: The level is between −20.5 and −27.0 dB at 0:45–1:20, with 2.0–4.2 detected onsets per second; the key estimate stays C major (0.80–0.94). The comparison with Songs Without Words is from Wikipedia’s article.

cues.title: A shift to A minor
cues.text: At about 1:25 the key estimate turns to A minor, the relative minor of C, and the detected note activity rises to five a second by 1:35. The music takes a darker turn, though the middle section proper has not yet begun.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is A minor (0.79–0.89) at 1:25–1:40 with the bass on A at 1:30–1:40; the report has a boundary at 1:26 (0.56); detected onsets are 3.6–5.2 per second. The estimate is approximate; the middle section proper is placed at 3:48 from a much larger change.

cues.title: A pause on G
cues.text: Around 1:55 the music rests on a G major sonority, the dominant of C: the level dips to −26 dB and the key estimate fits G major at 0.96. Listen for the sense of waiting before the music moves on.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is G major (0.89–0.96) at 1:50–2:00 with the bass on G, the level −24.3 dB at 1:50 and −26.4 dB at 1:55, and 1.0 detected onsets per second at 1:55; the report has a boundary at 1:50 (0.39). The estimates are approximate.

cues.title: A darker detour
cues.text: From about 2:10 to 2:30 the sound is louder and the harmony darkens: the key estimates pass through G minor, E♭ major and C minor with notes arriving at four or five a second. Listen for the colour changing before the theme returns.
cues.evidence: The key estimates are G minor (0.62) at 2:10, E♭ major (0.78–0.91) at 2:15–2:20 and C minor (0.78) at 2:25; the level is −15.2 to −17.8 dB with 4.0–5.2 detected onsets per second; the report has boundaries at 2:14 (0.66), 2:20 (0.45), 2:26 (0.93). The estimates are approximate.

cues.title: Back to C major
cues.text: At about 2:32, the strongest structural boundary in the file, the music leaves the dark detour and comes back to C major. The level falls about five decibels, then rises to −13.7 dB by 2:45 as the home key is confirmed.
cues.evidence: The report’s strongest boundary is at 2:32 (novelty 1.00); the level is −17.8 dB at 2:25, −22.2 dB at 2:30 and −20.2 dB at 2:35, then −13.7 dB at 2:45; the key estimate is C major (0.77–0.93) at 2:35–2:50.

cues.title: A song without words
cues.text: Wikipedia calls the Andante reminiscent of Mendelssohn’s own Songs Without Words, the short lyrical piano pieces he published in several books. The movement is in ternary form: a lyrical theme, a darker middle section and a return.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article on the concerto makes the comparison with the Songs Without Words and describes the ternary form; it is a descriptive comparison, not a documented borrowing.

cues.title: A friend as concertmaster
cues.text: After Mendelssohn became principal conductor of the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra in 1835, he made his childhood friend Ferdinand David its concertmaster. David advised on the violin writing while the concerto took shape, as their correspondence shows, and the concerto is dedicated to him.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article gives Mendelssohn’s 1835 appointment, David’s role as concertmaster and their correspondence about the violin writing; the IMSLP work page gives the dedication to David.

cues.title: The orchestra opens the middle section
cues.text: At about 3:48 the level jumps about ten decibels and the music turns to A minor. Wikipedia says the darker middle section’s theme is first introduced by the orchestra, and only then taken up by the violin.
cues.evidence: The level rises from −18.1 dB at 3:45 to −8.2 dB at 3:50 and −6.9 dB at 3:55; the report has a boundary at 3:48 (0.78); the key estimate is A minor (0.74) at 3:50 and A major (0.73–0.77) at 3:55–4:00. Wikipedia describes the A minor middle section and the orchestra’s first statement; the 3:50 and 3:55 windows are among the five loudest.

cues.title: Melody and accompaniment in one violin
cues.text: From about 4:05 the solo violin takes the theme and plays its own agitated accompaniment as well. Wikipedia describes a tremulous accompaniment that demands nimble dexterity, and the level falls as the soloist replaces the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: The level falls from −7.0 dB at 4:00 to −14.1 dB at 4:05 and −18.5 dB at 4:10, with detected onsets of 4.6–5.8 per second at 4:05–4:15; the key estimate is A major (0.74–0.88) at 4:05–4:15. Wikipedia describes the violin taking melody and accompaniment together.

cues.title: The loudest moment
cues.text: At about 4:30 the whole orchestra reaches the loudest window of the file, near −6 dB, with the detected note activity dropping to long chords. After a dip it returns at 4:40, so the middle section peaks twice.
cues.evidence: The level is −12.4 dB at 4:25, −6.1 dB at 4:30, −12.1 dB at 4:35 and −7.7 dB at 4:40; the 4:30 and 4:40 windows are among the five loudest; the report has boundaries at 4:42 (0.53) and 4:54 (0.45); detected onsets are 1.6 at 4:30 and 3.4 at 4:40.

cues.title: The densest figuration
cues.text: At 4:45–4:55 the detected note activity reaches its highest values in the file, five to seven a second. Listen for the violin’s fast, shivering accompaniment under the melody, which gives the middle section its restless sound.
cues.evidence: Detected onsets are 5.0 per second at 4:45, 6.8 at 4:50 and 5.8 at 4:55, the highest values in the file; the key estimate is A major/minor (0.67–0.81) at 4:45–4:55. Detected onsets are not note counts; the description of the figuration is from Wikipedia.

cues.title: The middle section dies away
cues.text: From about 5:25 the sound falls from −14 dB to −34 dB by 5:40, one of the quietest windows in the file. The minor-key energy drains away before the lyrical theme comes back in C major.
cues.evidence: The level is −13.8 dB at 5:25, −20.1 dB at 5:30, −24.7 dB at 5:35 and −33.5 dB at 5:40 (among the five quietest windows); the report has boundaries at 5:08 (0.45) and 5:34 (0.47).

cues.title: The lyrical theme returns
cues.text: At about 5:45 the key estimate is back in C major, and the main lyrical theme returns for the third part of the movement. Wikipedia says it now leads towards a serene conclusion.
cues.evidence: The key estimate is C major (0.66) at 5:45 and 0.79–0.87 from 5:50 to 6:15, with the bass on C or F; the level rises from −24.9 dB at 5:45 to −12.7 dB at 6:15. Wikipedia describes the return of the main lyrical C major theme and the serene conclusion.

cues.title: The return grows louder
cues.text: The returning theme swells more than it did the first time: from about 6:05 the level rises to −12.7 dB at 6:15, louder than anything in the first section, before easing again. Listen for the added warmth on this second hearing.
cues.evidence: The level is −15.2 dB at 6:05, −14.2 dB at 6:10 and −12.7 dB at 6:15, against −17 to −27 dB at 0:35–1:20 and −13.7 dB at 2:45; the key estimate is C major (0.82–0.95). This compares levels within one recording and does not measure dynamics.

cues.title: The first long-playing record
cues.text: When Columbia introduced the long-playing record in 1948, its first LP, ML 4001, was Nathan Milstein’s recording of this concerto with the New York Philharmonic under Bruno Walter. Wikipedia adds that the concerto is now virtually ubiquitous in the discography of concert violinists.
cues.evidence: The Library of Congress blog post “Inside the Archival Box: The First Long-Playing Disc” (https://blogs.loc.gov/now-see-hear/2019/04/inside-the-archival-box-the-first-long-playing-disc/) names the 1948 Columbia release ML 4001 with the Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra of New York, Bruno Walter and Nathan Milstein in this concerto, from Columbia’s label paperwork; its comments dispute which disc counts as first. Wikipedia’s article gives the 1948 release and the remark on the discography.

cues.title: A hush, then the theme moves on
cues.text: Around 7:10–7:20 the music nearly stops: the level dips to −27 dB with under one detected note a second, then at about 7:20 the accompaniment resumes in C major with the key estimate at 0.93. It is a breath before the closing paragraph.
cues.evidence: The level is −22.2 dB at 7:10, −26.6 dB at 7:15 with 0.8 detected onsets per second, and −19.6 dB at 7:20 with 4.8; the key estimate is C major (0.87–0.93) at 7:15–7:20.

cues.title: The serene close
cues.text: At about 8:00 the closing section begins: the level falls to about −27 dB and then −34 dB at 8:15, with almost no detected note activity. The music stays in C major to the last chord, as Wikipedia’s description of a serene conclusion suggests.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 8:02 (0.53); the level is −25.0 dB at 7:50, −31.6 dB at 7:55, −27.1 dB at 8:00 and −34.1 dB at 8:15, with 0.2–1.0 detected onsets per second at 8:00–8:20 apart from 2.4 at 8:05; the key estimate is C major (0.79–0.87).

cues.title: Where the file stops
cues.text: In the closing seconds the last chord fades, at about −30 dB, and the recording stops at about 8:23. In the score the movement is joined to the finale by a short passage for the soloist and strings, so these two movement files are cut at a join the composer wrote as continuous.
cues.evidence: The level is −34.1 dB at 8:15 and −29.7 dB at 8:20, with 0.2 detected onsets per second and the bass on C; the file ends at 8:22.9. Wikipedia says a brief transitional passage for solo violin and strings follows the second movement; the score (printed p. 36–37) runs the movements together with a fermata.

transitions.title: The bassoon’s B steps up to C
transitions.from: Link · held B and wind introduction
transitions.to: First section · the soloist’s lyrical theme, C major
transitions.how: The Andante is joined to the first movement without a pause. The bassoon sustains the B of the final E minor chord, then moves up a semitone to middle C. B is the leading note of C, so the held note works as a bridge: it resolves up a semitone into the new tonic. A short introduction follows in the orchestra, a flute line with other winds joining over low strings, while the bass moves through G and B before reaching C at about 0:35. The soloist’s lyrical C major theme begins at about 0:40.
transitions.evidence: Wikipedia describes the bassoon’s B moving up a semitone to middle C and the absence of a break; the score (printed pp. 27–28) shows the held B, then a wind introduction over low strings before the solo theme. The bass pitch class is B at 0:00–0:15, G at 0:25, B at 0:30 and C at 0:35, with the key estimate C major (0.85–0.94) from 0:35 and detected onsets rising from 0.0 to 3.4 per second at 0:40; the chroma does not separate the bassoon.

transitions.title: The orchestra lurches into A minor
transitions.from: First section · lyrical theme, C major
transitions.to: Middle section · A minor, orchestra then violin
transitions.how: After a long, lyrical first section in C major with episodes, the music turns at about 3:48 to the darker middle section. The level jumps about ten decibels as the orchestra introduces the A minor theme, the relative minor of C, and only then does the violin take up both the melody and its own tremulous accompaniment. The key relation is close (A minor shares its notes with C major) but the change of weight and colour is abrupt.
transitions.evidence: The level rises from −18.1 dB at 3:45 to −8.2 dB at 3:50 and −6.9 dB at 3:55, with a boundary at 3:48 (0.78) and the key estimate A minor (0.74) at 3:50. Wikipedia describes the A minor middle section, introduced by the orchestra before the violin takes the melody and accompaniment.

transitions.title: The agitation drains; the theme returns
transitions.from: Middle section · A minor, orchestra then violin
transitions.to: Return · the lyrical theme in C major
transitions.how: The middle section ends by dying away: the level falls from about −14 dB at 5:25 to −34 dB at 5:40 as the restless figuration thins. Then C major returns, and with it the main lyrical theme, now for the third part of the ternary form. The return is not marked by a loud cadence: the music empties, and the opening key and tune reappear in the quiet.
transitions.evidence: The level is −13.8 dB at 5:25, −24.7 dB at 5:35 and −33.5 dB at 5:40, with boundaries at 5:34 (0.47); the key estimate is C major (0.66) at 5:45 and 0.87 at 5:50. Wikipedia describes the return of the main lyrical C major theme.

transitions.title: A thinning toward the final chord
transitions.from: Return · the lyrical theme in C major
transitions.how: The returning theme runs its course and, at about 8:00, the music thins to a close: the level falls to about −27 dB and then −34 dB at 8:15, with almost no detected note activity and C as the bass. The key remains C major to the end, so the close is calm rather than dramatic. In the score a fermata on the last chord and a double bar lead straight into a short passage in E minor for the soloist and strings.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 8:02 (0.53); the level is −31.6 dB at 7:55, −27.1 dB at 8:00 and −34.1 dB at 8:15, with 0.2–1.0 detected onsets per second at 8:10–8:20 and the key estimate C major (0.79–0.87). The score (printed pp. 36–37) shows the last chord with a fermata followed by the Allegretto non troppo.

source.title: Mendelssohn, Violin Concerto in E minor, Op. 64, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel; Rietz edition, Serie 4 No. 18). The text this performance follows is not documented.
source.locator: II. Andante, printed pp. 27–36. The snapshots are read from printed pp. 27–28 (the introduction and the solo theme) and p. 31 (the fortissimo entry); the trumpets, timpani and string tremolos of the middle section follow Steven Ledbetter’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note (https://www.bso.org/works/mendelssohn-violin-concerto); the other entries follow Wikipedia’s description.

timeline.note: The bassoon’s held B from the first movement, before it moves to C.
The Andante opens with a flute line, other winds joining over low strings; the soloist rests.
The soloist’s lyrical C major theme over a moving string accompaniment.
The orchestra introduces the A minor theme at fortissimo, the soloist joining the first chord, before the violin takes the theme up (printed p. 31).
The soloist takes the A minor theme and plays its own tremulous accompaniment, according to Wikipedia.
At the middle section’s peaks the whole orchestra sounds with the soloist; the trumpets and timpani, seconded by string tremolos, give the movement its darkest colour (Ledbetter, BSO note).
The main lyrical theme returns in C major.

composer.epithet: A composer-conductor who turned quicksilver string writing, Bachian counterpoint and remembered landscapes into tightly organised concert music.
facts: Piano with Ludwig Berger; composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter in Berlin
Music director, Düsseldorf, 1833–35; Gewandhaus conductor, Leipzig, from 1835; founder of Leipzig Conservatoire, 1843
Brother of Fanny Hensel; married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children
Symphonies, concert overtures, concertos, oratorios, chamber music and Songs without Words
composer.background:
Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 and grew up in Berlin, where his father Abraham’s banking wealth supported an unusually extensive education. His grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn; Felix and his siblings were baptised as Christians in 1816, and the family used the additional surname Bartholdy. He studied piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter, alongside his elder sister Fanny. The family’s concerts extended their classroom education with repeated opportunities to hear their own music, revise it and discuss it with experienced performers.

Zelter’s teaching joined Bach’s counterpoint to classical forms. The boy wrote string symphonies, concertos and chamber works before the pieces usually treated as his starting point. At sixteen he composed the E♭ major Octet, Op. 20, for four violins, two violas and two cellos. Its eight independent parts create different densities inside one ensemble: the first violin’s long ascent, the other instruments’ pulsing accompaniments and the finale’s fugal entries continually reshape the texture. The scherzo’s soft, rapid articulation became a recurrent technical problem in his later orchestral writing.
